passages.title: The oaths and their answer: your strivings diverge
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

Sūrah al-Layl opens with three oaths — by the night, by the day, and by the One who created male and female — and then delivers what they were sworn upon: **"Surely the ends you strive for are diverse"** (ayah 4). The oaths are not decoration. Ibn Kathir draws out the logic in a single sentence: *"just as these things that are being sworn by are opposites, likewise that which this swearing is about are opposing things."* Allah swears by things that come in opposed pairs in order to say that human striving, too, comes in opposed kinds.

That is what holds ayat 1–4 together. Three witnesses are called, and all three testify to the same truth: **opposition and pairing are woven into creation itself, and your own striving is part of that pattern.**

Ibn Kathir titles this stretch of the sūrah *"Swearing by the Diversity of Mankind in Their Efforts and informing of the Different Results of that."* That title is a good map of the whole passage.

---

## Ayah 1 — "By the night when it covers"

Ibn Kathir glosses **wa'l-layli idhā yaghshā** as: *"when it covers the creation with its darkness."*

Notice how much is packed into that short gloss. What the night covers is *the creation* — not one place, not one household, but everything laid out under it. And what it covers creation with is *its darkness*: whatever was distinct and visible a moment ago is now under one sheet of shadow.

This is the first half of the pair, and Allah puts the dark half first.

---

## Ayah 2 — "and the day when it shines"

**Wa'n-nahāri idhā tajallā** — Ibn Kathir: *"with its light and its radiance."*

Where the night came over the creation with darkness, the day comes with light and radiance. Concealing, then disclosing. What darkness had merged into one indistinguishable mass, light lays back out in view.

Read the two ayat together and you have the most familiar sight any human being has ever had: the covering of the night and the shining of the day, turn and turn about. It is a rhythm no one escapes and no one arranged for himself. And it is placed here as a witness — the first pair of opposites called to testify.

---

## Ayah 3 — "And by ˹the One˺ Who created male and female"

The third oath moves from the sky to the human being — but notice, it does not swear by male and female. It swears by **the One who created them**. Ibn Kathir renders it *"By Him Who created male and female,"* and the translation before you does the same: the oath lands on the Creator, not the creation.

Ibn Kathir connects this to two other places in the Qur'an where the same theme appears:

- *"And We have created you in pairs"* (78:8)
- *"And of everything We have created pairs"* (51:49)

That second one is the widest statement of all: pairing is not a quirk of biology, it runs through *everything*. Night and day are a pair. Male and female are a pair. And on Ibn Kathir's reading, the pairing is not accidental — it is what Allah *created*. The oath by the Creator in ayah 3 quietly answers a question the first two oaths raise: who set this up? The One who is now swearing by it.

**Why this matters for the answer to come.** The three oaths build a case. If pairing and opposition are real and deliberate in the cosmos and in the human being's own making, then it is no surprise that they should be real in what human beings *do*. Ayah 4 is not an arbitrary claim dropped on the reader. It has been prepared for by three witnesses.

---

## Ayah 4 — the answer: "Surely the ends you strive for are diverse"

**Inna saʿyakum la-shattā.** Ibn Kathir renders it *"Certainly, your efforts and deeds are diverse,"* and explains: *"the actions of the servants that they have performed are also opposites and diverse. Therefore, there are those who do good and there are those who do evil."*

Two things are worth pausing on in that gloss.

First, the diversity Ibn Kathir has in mind is not mere variety — it is *opposition*. He says the actions are "opposites and diverse," matching the opposites sworn by in ayat 1–3. The night and the day are not two flavours of the same thing; they are contraries. So it is with human striving.

Second, he immediately cashes this out in the plainest possible terms: *there are those who do good and there are those who do evil.* No abstraction. Two kinds of people, sorted by what they do.

And note who is addressed: **your** efforts. Ibn Kathir speaks of "the actions of the servants" — this is a statement about people at large, and everyone reciting it is inside it. Nobody is a spectator to this ayah.

### Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: everyone is working; the question is what for

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān links this ayah to the statement in Sūrah al-Inshiqāq: *"O man, you have to work hard constantly to reach your Lord"* (84:6), and draws out the point:

> "Man, by his nature, is used to making efforts for one objective or another. But the nature and the results of these efforts are different. Some people work hard for an objective that brings eternal happiness to them, and others work hard for an objective that makes them suffer eternal perdition."

This is the heart of the passage, and it is worth sitting with. The ayah does not divide humanity into the hardworking and the lazy. Everyone in it is *making efforts*. The tireless and the driven are on both sides of the line. Effort by itself proves nothing and saves nobody; what settles a life is **what the effort is aimed at**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then relates that it is reported in a Tradition that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that each morning when a man gets up, he goes to conduct his business and keeps himself busy — and his business is either successful, and so emancipates him from Hell, or unsuccessful, so that his efforts become the cause of his destruction. *(The commentary conveys this teaching without naming the collection it comes from, so it is given here only as the commentary gives it.)*

Every ordinary morning is therefore a transaction with the Hereafter. There is no neutral day.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a plainly practical conclusion:

> "A wise person should first apply his mind to think whether his efforts will pay dividends, and he should never undertake those efforts that bring about temporary comfort and pleasure, but eternal perdition and grief."

---

## Where the passage is heading

Ayah 4 states the divergence; the ayat that follow name the two directions. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the Qur'an goes on to show that "broadly speaking, the humankind may be divided into two opposing groups in terms of their opposing efforts," each marked by three qualities — one group successful, the other not. Ibn Kathir's own heading for the passage promises exactly this: the swearing is about the diversity of mankind in their efforts, "and informing of the Different Results of that."

Those two groups, and the results Allah decrees for each, are the business of the ayat that follow. Here the sūrah has only made the claim; next it will draw the two portraits.

---

## Living it

**Audit the direction, not the intensity.** Ayah 4 does not ask whether you are working hard. It assumes you are. It asks where the effort is aimed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's counsel is exactly this: think first about whether the effort will pay, and refuse the effort that buys temporary comfort at the price of lasting loss.

**Take the morning seriously.** In the teaching Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, the man's day is not a blank stretch of time — it is a business that either frees him or ruins him. That reframes an ordinary Tuesday.

**Let the night and day preach.** These are the two sights every person sees daily. After this sūrah, the covering of the night and the shining of the day are no longer neutral scenery; they are Allah's own chosen witnesses that things really do come in opposed pairs — and that human striving is one of those things.

**A note on this sūrah in prayer.** Ibn Kathir opens his commentary here under the heading *"The Recitation of Surat Al-Layl in the 'Isha' Prayer,"* recalling the Prophet's ﷺ words to Muʿādh, when he asked him why he had not prayed with Sūrah al-Aʿlā (87), Sūrah ash-Shams (91), and Sūrah al-Layl (92) — the sūrah whose opening we are reading. *(Ibn Kathir refers back to this statement without naming a collection at this point, so it is reported here only as he reports it.)*

passages.title: Two paths: the giver and the miser
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat take the surah's opening claim — that human striving is not all one thing — and split humanity in two. Ayat 5–7 describe one kind of person and where they end up; ayat 8–10 describe their opposite and where *they* end up; ayah 11 closes the second portrait with a question that empties the miser's hands. What holds the passage together is its symmetry: three traits and one outcome, mirrored twice.

## The setup: a world built on opposites

Ibn Kathir points out that the oaths just before this passage are all *pairs of opposites* — the night as it envelops, "when it covers the creation with its darkness," and the day as it appears, "with its light and its radiance," and then "By Him Who created male and female." He compares this to Allah's words elsewhere: "And We have created you in pairs" (78:8), and "And of everything We have created pairs" (51:49). Then he draws the conclusion that unlocks everything after it: *just as the things sworn by are opposites, so is the thing sworn about.* That is why ayah 4 says your efforts are diverse — meaning, in Ibn Kathir's words, that the deeds of the servants "are also opposites and diverse. Therefore, there are those who do good and there are those who do evil."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets ayah 4 beside "O man, you have to work hard constantly to reach your Lord" (84:6) and draws out the human reality underneath: by nature, everyone is exerting themselves toward *something*. Nobody is idle. The difference is never effort versus no effort — it is what the effort is aimed at. "Some people work hard for an objective that brings eternal happiness to them, and others work hard for an objective that makes them suffer eternal perdition." Maʿārif relates that it is reported the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that each morning a man rises and goes about his business, and either that business succeeds and frees him from Hell, or it fails and his own efforts become the cause of his destruction. (The source relates this without naming a collection, so take it as the teaching it conveys rather than as a citation.) The practical upshot Maʿārif draws is blunt: a wise person thinks *first* about whether his efforts will pay dividends, and never undertakes efforts that bring temporary comfort and pleasure but eternal perdition and grief.

So the passage lays out its two portraits side by side: "As for him who gives and has Taqwa" (ayah 5), and then, matching it phrase for phrase, "But he who is greedy and thinks himself self-sufficient" (ayah 8). Two people, two sets of three traits, two destinations.

## Three qualities on each side

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the passage as dividing humankind into two opposing groups, each marked by three characteristics.

**The successful group** (ayat 5–6): they give in charity in the cause of Allah; they fear Allah and avoid violating His injunctions in every aspect of life; and they believe in *al-ḥusnā*.

**The unsuccessful group** (ayat 8–9): they are misers to the point that they even fail to pay zakah and other obligatory alms; they deem themselves self-sufficient rather than obeying Allah; and they reject *al-ḥusnā*.

Notice how much is packed into how little. Ibn Kathir explains "he gives" as meaning "he gives what he has been commanded to give" — not whatever he feels like parting with, but what is due. And of "and has Taqwa," Ibn Kathir says it means "he fears Allah in his affairs." Taqwa, then, is that fear of Allah which shows up in how a person conducts himself; Maʿārif spells it out as fearing Allah and avoiding violation of His injunctions "in every aspect of life," not merely in the moment of giving. The pairing matters: giving *plus* taqwa. Both commentaries hold the two together, and the surah does not let us take one without the other.

## What is *al-ḥusnā*?

Our two commentaries explain *al-ḥusnā* in two ways, each reported from early authorities.

**Reading one — the reward.** Ibn Kathir reports that Qatadah understood it as "the compensation for that," and Khusayf said "in the reward." Commenting on ayah 9, Ibn Kathir glosses the denial of al-ḥusnā as denying "the recompense in the abode of the Hereafter." On this reading, the giver gives *because* he is certain that what Allah has promised is real — his hand opens because his heart has already accepted the Hereafter.

**Reading two — the best word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, as explained by Ibn ʿAbbās and Ḍaḥḥāk, that al-ḥusnā refers to "the best word," the credo *lā ilāha illā Allāh* — "there is no god but Allah." Testifying to the kalimah, Maʿārif says, signifies professing the true faith.

Maʿārif then raises a question worth sitting with. If faith is "the essence of all actions" and "comes first in order of rank," why is it mentioned *last* in each triplet, after giving and taqwa? Its answer: probably because the main theme running through this passage is physical exertion — efforts and actions. Faith, by contrast, "pertains to the heart. It signifies the acceptance and confirmation of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ with one's heart," confessed by reciting the kalimah shahādah. None of that involves physical exertion, and such things "are not generally counted as actions." So it is placed at the end of a list otherwise made of actions — last in the sentence, first in rank.

## The miser: stingy with wealth, and with need

Ayah 8 gives the mirror image. Of "But he who is greedy," Ibn Kathir explains, simply, "with that which he has." Maʿārif sharpens it: a miserliness so entrenched that even obligatory zakah goes unpaid.

Then comes the phrase that exposes the disease beneath the symptom: "and thinks himself self-sufficient." ʿIkrimah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās — recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim, as Ibn Kathir relates — that this means "he is stingy with his wealth and considers himself to be in no need of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic."

That is the heart of the whole portrait. Miserliness here is not merely a money problem; the closed hand is paired with a soul that has concluded it does not need its Lord. Maʿārif puts the same thing in terms of obedience: they "deem themselves self-sufficient rather than obeying Allah."

And this is why ayah 11 lands where it does. The man who considered himself in no need of his Lord is the very man who is asked, at the close of the passage, "And what will his wealth avail him when he goes down?"

## "We will make smooth for him the path of ease"

The two outcomes are stated in matching words with opposite destinations: "We will make smooth for him the path of ease" (ayah 7) and "We will make smooth for him the path to evil" (ayah 10).

On the first, Ibn Kathir reports Ibn ʿAbbās as saying it means "for goodness." Maʿārif explains that *yusrā* literally denotes "ease and comfort," a thing in which there is no difficulty — and here refers to Paradise; while its opposite, *ʿusrā*, literally denotes extreme distress, referring to Hell. Ibn Kathir glosses the second as "the path of evil," citing as a parallel: "And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away, as they refused to believe therein for the first time, and We shall leave them in their trespass to wander blindly" (6:110). His summary of the principle: "Allah rewards those who intend good with success, while whoever intends evil is abandoned."

Maʿārif catches a subtlety that is easy to walk past. By rights, it says, it should have been said that the *deeds* of Paradise or Hell are made easy for them, "because 'easy' or 'difficult' qualify deeds, and not persons or people." But the Qur'an says the people themselves will be made easy toward the deeds. Maʿārif suggests this probably implies a settled disposition: the first group will be so predisposed toward good that behaving otherwise will make them feel uneasy, while the second will feel comfortable doing the deeds of Hell and uneasy doing the deeds of Paradise. Each group will have "their own nature and predisposition, and will find it easier to behave in that particular way."

Habits of obedience, on this reading, are not merely repeated acts — they reshape what feels easy.

## Does this mean it is all already decided?

Ibn Kathir says all of this is "in accordance with a preordained decree," and gathers a cluster of narrations in which the Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ this exact question:

- **Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq** asked whether we act according to what has already been decided or whether the matter is still undecided. The Prophet ﷺ answered, "Indeed it is according to what has already been decided." Abu Bakr then asked: then what good are deeds? He ﷺ replied, "Everyone will find it easy to do such deeds that will lead him to what he was created for." *(Recorded by Imam Ahmad.)*

- **ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib** narrated that they were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at a funeral in the cemetery of Baqīʿ al-Gharqad. He sat down and they sat around him; he had a stick with him, and he bowed his head and began scratching the ground with it. Then he said that there is not a single soul except that its place in Paradise or the Fire has been written, and that it has been written whether it will be miserable or happy. A man said: then should we simply depend on what has been written and give up performing deeds? He ﷺ replied, "Those people who are the people of happiness, they will have the deeds of the people of happiness made easy for them. And those people who are the people of misery, they will have the deeds of the people of misery made easy for them" — and then he recited these very ayat, from "As for him who gives and has Taqwa" through "the path to evil." In a similar narration his answer begins, "Perform deeds, for everyone will have the deeds of what he was created for made easy for him." *(Recorded by al-Bukhari; Ibn Kathir notes that the other compilers of the Group also recorded it.)*

- **ʿUmar** asked the same, and was told: "It is something that has already been predetermined. Therefore, work deeds, O son of al-Khaṭṭāb! For verily, each person will have things made easy for him." *(Imam Ahmad recorded it from Ibn ʿUmar; at-Tirmidhi recorded it in the Book of al-Qadar and said "Hasan Sahih.")*

- **Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh** narrated the same exchange, and when Surāqah asked what the purpose of deeds is, the Prophet ﷺ said, "Everyone who does deeds will have his deeds made easy for him." *(Recorded by Ibn Jarir; Muslim also recorded it.)*

Look carefully at the pattern in these narrations. The question is always "so why act?" — and the answer is never "you needn't." In ʿAlī's narration it begins with a command: *Perform deeds*. In ʿUmar's it is sharper still: *work deeds, O son of al-Khaṭṭāb*. And the Prophet ﷺ recited these ayat as the answer, because the ayat themselves describe an action-shaped person on each side.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the other half plainly, immediately after quoting the same hadith wording: both of these outcomes are the result of the use of the choice and free will Allah has given, and that is precisely why man is rewarded or punished. So Ibn Kathir affirms the preordained decree and Maʿārif affirms genuine choice and genuine accountability — and the Companions' questions show that this tension is old and honest, and that the Prophet's ﷺ answer was not a theory to master but a command to obey: work.

## Abu Bakr and the ayah

Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Jarir, from ʿĀmir bin ʿAbdullāh bin az-Zubayr, that Abu Bakr used to free servants in Makkah upon their acceptance of Islam — the elderly and the women among them. His father said to him: my son, I see you freeing people who are weak; if you freed strong men, they could stand with you, defend you, and protect you. Abu Bakr replied: "O my father! I only want… what is with Allah."

The narrator adds — and the wording is careful — "Some people of my family have told me this Ayah was revealed about him: *As for him who gives and has Taqwa, and believes in al-Ḥusnā. We will make smooth for him the path of ease.*"

Set the story against the ayah and every phrase lights up. He *gave* — and gave where no worldly return was in view. He had *taqwa* — his father's calculation of political advantage never moved him. And he *believed in al-ḥusnā* — which is the entire content of "I only want what is with Allah."

## What will his wealth avail him?

The passage ends with the miser's account closed: "And what will his wealth avail him when he goes down?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *taraddā* literally denotes "to fall into a pit and perish," and that the expression signifies that when the divine decree concerning his destruction comes into operation, nothing — not even his wealth — will save him, "whether in grave after his death, or on the Day of Judgment, when he will be falling into the abyss of Hell."

Ibn Kathir reports the same phrase explained two ways: Mujahid said, "This means when he dies"; and Abu Salih and Malik said, narrating from Zayd bin Aslam, "When he goes down into the Fire."

The image is of a man tumbling, and everything he clutched staying behind. He withheld his wealth precisely because he thought it made him secure. It cannot follow him a single step past the edge.

## Living it

- **Give what you have been commanded to give.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 5 makes what is due the floor, not the ceiling. Maʿārif's description of the second group begins exactly there: misers who "even fail to pay the zakah."
- **Audit the heart behind the closed hand.** Ibn ʿAbbās diagnosed the miser as one who "considers himself to be in no need of his Lord." If you find yourself unwilling to give, the question is not only how much you have but whether you have quietly started believing you are self-sufficient.
- **Ask what your striving is buying.** Everyone strives, says Maʿārif; the only question is toward what. Think the return through *before* committing your effort, and never trade eternal perdition for temporary comfort.
- **Never let decree become an excuse.** Every Companion who asked "so why act?" was answered with the deeds themselves: perform them; work.
- **Trust the promise you cannot see.** Believing in al-ḥusnā — whether read as the recompense of the Hereafter or as the kalimah itself — is what makes a hand open when nothing visible is coming back. That is what Abu Bakr meant by "I only want what is with Allah."

passages.title: Guidance is Ours, so the Fire is a warning
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

These five ayat move in one direction. Allah says that showing the way to guidance is upon Him (12), that both worlds — this one and the next — belong to Him (13), and then comes the warning: **"And so I have warned you of a raging Fire"** (14). Ayat 15 and 16 then say who enters that Fire, and Allah does not leave us to guess: **"the most wretched"** is defined in the very next line as **the one who denied and turned away.**

Ibn Kathir gathers all of this under one heading: *"The Matter of Guidance and other than it is in the Hand of Allah, and Allah's Warning about the Hellfire."* Both halves of that heading matter — the guidance and the warning are being treated together, as one subject.

---

## "It is certainly upon Us ˹alone˺ to show ˹the way to˺ guidance" (12)

Notice the wording: guidance is something Allah speaks of as being *upon Us*.

The early commentators read this in two complementary ways, both preserved by Ibn Kathir:

**Qatadah** said it means: *"We will explain what is lawful and what is prohibited."* On this reading, guidance is Allah making the path clear — drawing the line between the lawful and the forbidden, so that a person is not left in the dark about which way to walk.

**Others** said it means: *"Whoever traverses upon the path of guidance, then he will reach Allah"* — that is, in the Hereafter. The road is guaranteed to arrive; the traveller on it is not wasting his steps. Ibn Kathir notes that this group read the ayah alongside Allah's saying, **"And upon Allah is the responsibility to explain the Straight path"** (16:9), and he says this has been mentioned by Ibn Jarir.

Neither reading cancels the other. One tells you the way has been made plain; the other tells you the destination is real.

## "And surely to Us ˹alone˺ belong this life and the next" (13)

Ibn Kathir's comment is short and total: *"they both belong to Us and I (Allah) am in complete control of them."*

Notice how this closes off every escape route. A person might accept that the next world belongs to Allah while quietly living as though this one belongs to him. Ayah 13 refuses the split. The last and the first — the Hereafter and this world — are named together and assigned to one Owner, in complete control of both.

---

## "A raging Fire" — and the way the Prophet ﷺ delivered the warning (14)

The Arabic word Ibn Kathir preserves untranslated is **Talazza**. **Mujahid** glossed it in a single word: *"Blazing."*

The warning itself is spoken in the first person: *"And so **I** have warned you."*

And the Prophet ﷺ took those words onto his own tongue. Imam Ahmad recorded from Simak bin Harb that he heard An-Nu'man bin Bashir giving a sermon in which he said:

> "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ giving a sermon, in which he said: **'I have warned you of the Fire.'** And he said it in such a voice that if a man was in the marketplace he could hear it from where I am standing now. And he said it (with such force) that the garment that was on his shoulder fell down to his feet."

Sit with that scene. A man in the market — not in the mosque, not listening, busy with his buying and selling — could hear it. The Prophet ﷺ pushed his voice until the cloak slid from his shoulder to his feet. This is what it looked like when a heart that truly understood this warning tried to make other people understand it. It was not read out; it was called out, at cost to the one calling.

### The lightest punishment

Ibn Kathir then brings two narrations that measure the Fire not from its depths but from its shallowest edge.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Ishaq that he heard An-Nu'man bin Bashir say that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

> "Verily, the person to be punished lightest of the people of the Fire on the Day of Judgement will be a man who will have placed on the soles of his feet two coals that will cause his brain to boil."

Ibn Kathir notes that **Imam Al-Bukhari also recorded this narration**. And **Muslim** recorded, from Abu Ishaq from An-Nu'man bin Bashir, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Verily, the lightest punishment received by the people of the Hellfire will be a man who will have two sandals whose straps will be made of fire that will cause his brain to boil just as a cauldron boils. Yet he will not think that anyone is receiving a torment more severe than him, even though he will be receiving the lightest punishment of them."

Two things are being taught. First, the sheer distance between two coals under the feet and a mind boiling like a pot — the Fire is not on a human scale. Second, and more sobering: the man receiving the lightest punishment does not think anyone is worse off than he is. Suffering fills the whole horizon of the one suffering. Nobody in the Fire is comforted by knowing that others have it worse.

---

## "In which none will burn except the most wretched" (15–16)

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase this way: *"none will enter surrounded by it on all sides except the most wretched."* Entering, here, means being surrounded by the Fire — not merely brushing past it.

Then Allah, in ayah 16, defines this person with two words, and Ibn Kathir unpacks each one precisely:

- **"Who denies"** — *"meaning, in his heart."*
- **"and turns away"** — *"meaning, from acting with his limbs and performing deeds according to their pillars."*

So the description covers the whole person: the inward act of calling the truth a lie, and the outward act of walking away from what one owes. Denial in the heart, desertion in the limbs.

### Turning away is a refusal

Ibn Kathir places here a hadith that names what is really happening. Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "All of my followers will enter Paradise on the Day of Judgement except for whoever refuses."

The Companions said, "Who would refuse, O Messenger of Allah?" He replied:

> "Whoever obeys me, he will enter Paradise, and whoever disobeys me, then he has refused."

Ibn Kathir notes that **Al-Bukhari also recorded this Hadith**. The word *refuses* is the key. To turn away is not an oversight; the Prophet ﷺ names disobedience itself as refusal — which brings us back to ayah 12, where Qatadah said Allah's undertaking was to explain what is lawful and what is prohibited.

---

## A serious question the scholars addressed

Read plainly, ayah 15 seems to say that **only** the denier-and-turner-away will enter the Fire. Maarif ul Quran raises this squarely: it is quite clear that only a *kafir* (a disbeliever) rejects Allah and His Messenger — so, apparently, a sinful believer who does not reject the truth would not enter Hell. Yet, as Maarif notes, "the Qur'an and Hadith are replete with clear texts that a sinful believer will enter Hell, unless he had repented, or someone interceded for him, or was forgiven out of pure Grace." Such a person abides there until he has received the punishment for the sins he has committed; then, after paying for his sins, "he will be taken out of Hell, and through the blessings of his faith, he will be admitted into Paradise."

Because the apparent wording seems contrary to this, Maarif says the ayah must be brought in line with other Qur'anic verses and authentic Ahadith. Its own "plain and simple interpretation" is that **the ayah refers to entering Hell for good** — permanent residence, which "is peculiar to the unbelievers," who "will be tortured eternally in the Hell-fire." Sinful believers, by contrast, receive punishment for their sins and "will eventually — at some time or the other — be taken out of Hell."

Maarif is careful to add that "other scholars of Tafsir have given some other interpretations too, which can also be appropriate," and it reports one of them: **Tafsir Mazhari** holds that the wretched one and the most Allah-fearing one should not be taken in the general sense at all, but refer particularly to people who lived during the blessed time of the Prophet ﷺ — such that no Muslim who lived at that time will enter Hell, through the blessings of his company, even though he might have committed some sins incidentally.

This is a place where the commentators genuinely differ, and it is right to hold their views as views rather than flattening them into one.

### The safety of the Companions

Maarif develops the point under the heading "All of The Blessed Companions will be Saved from the Ordeal of Hell": the Companions rarely ever committed sins; even if they did, their living conditions indicate they would have repented out of fear of the Hereafter; and their good deeds are so many that they can wipe out a sin, as Allah says, **"Surely good deeds erase bad deeds"** (11:114). Adopting the company of the Prophet ﷺ, it says, is itself an act that can outweigh all other good deeds. It reports that the Prophet ﷺ said regarding the righteous members of the community:

> "The one who sits with them is never deprived, and the one who feels happy in their company is never unsuccessful." [Sahihain]

Maarif also grounds this in the Qur'an: **"and to each Allah has promised good"** (4:95), and **"Surely, those for whom the good (news) from Us has come earlier shall be kept far away from it"** (21:101) — where *Husna*, "the good," refers to Paradise, and "it" refers to Hell. And it reports: "A Tradition says that 'Hell-Fire will not touch him who has seen me'." [Tirmidhi transmitted it from Jabir]

---

## Living it

**Treat guidance as something given, not something achieved.** Ayah 12 says the showing of the way is upon Allah, and Qatadah reads that as His explaining what is lawful and what is prohibited. What is left to you is to walk it. If you can tell halal from haram today, that clarity was handed to you.

**Do not let this world quietly detach from the next in your mind.** Ayah 13 puts both under one ownership, and Ibn Kathir's words are "complete control of them." The same Lord you will meet at the end is the Lord of your Monday morning.

**Take the warning as care, not cruelty.** Allah says "I have warned you" — and the Prophet ﷺ raised that same warning until his cloak fell from his shoulder. A warning delivered with that much effort is concern for the hearer. The one who tells you a road ends at a cliff is not your enemy.

**Guard the two doors named in ayah 16.** The heart that denies, and the limbs that turn away. Ibn Kathir locates the first "in his heart" and the second in "acting with his limbs." Keep both facing the same direction.

**Never be casual about "small" punishment.** The man with the burning sandal-straps does not think anyone is receiving a torment more severe than his — and he is the lightest of them. Any degree of that Fire is more than a person is built to carry, which is exactly why the warning was given while there is still time to heed it.

passages.title: The godfearing who gives for Allah alone
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close Sūrah al-Layl with a portrait: the person who will be kept far from the Fire. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the design plainly — this verse describes the reward of the most Allah-fearing person, as opposed to the punishment of the most wretched in the preceding verse. Ayah 17 names him; the ayat that follow describe him; and the sūrah ends on a single promise — **he will be pleased**.

## Ayah 17: *al-atqā* — the most Allah-fearing

Ibn Kathir glosses the ayah simply: **"the righteous, pure, most pious person will be saved from the Fire."** The renderings all speak of distance rather than a narrow escape — "will be spared from it," and, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "will be kept far away from the fire of Hell." He is not merely let off; he is held clear of it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the exact word used: **the word *atqā* is the superlative form and signifies a man of *taqwā* — that is, the most Allah-fearing person.** A superlative — not merely Allah-fearing, but the *most* Allah-fearing.

And who is that? The Qur'an does not leave it abstract. Ibn Kathir notes the movement of the passage: after naming him, **"He explains who he is by His saying"** — and what follows in ayat 18, 19 and 20 is the explanation. The description is spelled out in deeds and in intention.

## The story behind these ayat

This is where the passage opens up, because the sources tell us who was walking the streets of Makkah when it came down.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, citing **Ibn Abi Hatim from Sayyidnā ʿUrwah**, that seven Muslims had been enslaved by the Makkan disbelievers. When they became Muslims, they were persecuted in a variety of ways. Sayyidnā Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq spent a great amount of his own money, purchased them, and set them free. **Ayat 17–21 were revealed on this occasion** (attributed there to *Mazharī*).

Picture what that actually was. They were owned, and they were being tormented after becoming Muslims. Abu Bakr's response was not a speech. He paid — and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds from **the Mustadrak of Hakim**, this was his settled habit: he used to purchase Muslim slaves from the disbelievers and set them free whenever he found them in bondage. Generally, it records, these people were **weak and helpless**.

The same source preserves the conversation that goes to the heart of ayat 19 and 20. His father, Abu Qahāfah, said to him:

> "Since you are emancipating slaves, why do you not set free strong and brave people, so that they may assist you in fighting the enemies and protect you."

It is a shrewd question. If you must spend that much, buy men who can stand at your side. Abu Bakr answered:

> "My purpose of emancipating them is not to expect any benefit in return. My only purpose is to seek the pleasure of Allah."

That answer is ayat 19 and 20 in a man's own voice.

## Ayah 18: giving as purification

*"He who gives of his wealth for self-purification."*

Ibn Kathir unpacks the scope of it: he spends his wealth in obedience of his Lord **"in order to purify himself, his wealth and whatever Allah has bestowed upon him of religion and worldly things."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point more tightly — he spends in obedience of his Lord "in order to purify himself from sins."

So on Ibn Kathir's reading three things are washed clean by the same act: the giver, the wealth itself, and everything Allah has given him of religion and of this world. This is worth pausing on, because it inverts the ordinary logic of charity. We tend to think of giving as something the poor person needs. Here it is presented as something **the giver** needs. The wealth leaves; the impurity leaves with it.

## Ayah 19: the gift that pays back nothing

*"And who has (in mind) no favour from anyone to be paid back."*

Ibn Kathir explains: giving his wealth "is not done so that he may gain some favour from someone wherein they return some good to him, and therefore he gives to get something in return."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies it straight to the occasion: **the emancipated slaves had not done him any favour in the past**, so that no one could say he was merely returning their favour.

Ayah 19 is therefore doing something precise. Ayah 18 told us *what* he does. Ayah 19 clears away the worldly explanation of *why* — so that ayah 20 can supply the one that remains.

Ibn Kathir shows how deeply this ran in Abu Bakr with a moment from the day of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. ʿUrwah bin Masʿūd, chief of the tribe of Thaqīf, said to him: *"By Allah, if I did not owe you a debt, which I have not paid you back for, I would have responded to you"* — that is, to your call to Islam. **Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq became angry with him for saying such a thing.** He did not want a chief of the Arabs standing in his debt. Ibn Kathir's comment is pointed: if this was his position with the chiefs of the Arabs and the heads of the tribes, then what about those other than them?

Anyone who has given money and then felt, however faintly, that the recipient now owes them something — a greeting, a loyalty, a favour later — knows exactly what ayah 19 is cutting away.

## Ayah 20: seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High

Ibn Kathir renders the words "to seek the **Face** of his Lord, the Most High"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders them "to seek the **Countenance** of his Lord, the Most High." The translation given with the ayah itself reads "but seeking the pleasure of their Lord, the Most High."

And Ibn Kathir tells us what the seeker is actually hoping for: **"hoping to attain the blessing of seeing Him in the final abode in the Gardens of Paradise."**

That transforms the passage. Abu Bakr was not buying a reward he could hold. He was reaching, on Ibn Kathir's reading, for a *sight* — in a place he had not yet arrived at, from his Lord, the Most High. It is the last word the sūrah gives on why he gave.

Ibn Kathir says the same of his whole life of spending: "How many Dirhams and Dinars did he spend seeking the Face of His Most Noble Lord."

## Ayah 21: "He, surely, will be pleased"

Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief: "indeed those with these characteristics will be pleased." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the ayah "And surely he will soon be happy" — the promise is set ahead of him, and it is coming.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws out both halves of it. Generally: whoever spends in Allah's way with pure and good intentions of pleasing Allah, and not for any personal worldly gains, "will acquire the pleasure of Allah in the Hereafter by achieving the wonderful and eternal blessings of Paradise." And particularly: since it is confirmed that these ayat were revealed about Sayyidnā Abu Bakr, **this last ayah of the sūrah is a great and splendid news and honour for him given in this very world by Allah.**

Consider the symmetry. He gave, expecting nothing back from any creature — and the sūrah ends by telling him, in the Book that will be recited until the Last Day, that he will be pleased.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on this sūrah with a scene that fits it exactly. In **the Two Ṣaḥīḥs** it is recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever equipped two riding animals in the way of Allah, the Gatekeepers of Paradise will call to him saying, 'O servant of Allah! This is good.'"

Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah! The one who is called from them will not have any need. Will there be anyone who will be called from all of them?" The Prophet ﷺ replied:

> "Yes, and I hope that you will be one of them."

## Is this only about Abu Bakr?

The sources handle this carefully, and it matters for the reader.

Ibn Kathir reports that **many of the scholars of tafsīr** mentioned that these ayat were revealed about Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, and that some even mentioned a consensus among the Qur'anic commentators concerning it. His own verdict: there is no doubt that Abu Bakr is included in the meaning of these ayat and is the most deserving of the Ummah to be described with these characteristics — "for indeed, the wording of these Ayat is general." He was the first and foremost of this Ummah to have all of them, and other praiseworthy characteristics as well: truthful, pious, generous, charitable, always spending his wealth in obedience of his Master and in aiding the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same from the other direction: **"the wordings of the verse give good news, in general, to anyone who spends in Allah's cause in a state of faith,"** while the occasion of revelation indicates that *atqā* refers to Sayyidnā Abu Bakr in particular.

So the door is open. The description was *earned* by one man, and it is *offered* to anyone who will meet it.

## Living it

The passage sets out a test with three parts, and it is unusually easy to apply honestly.

**What leaves your hand.** Ayah 18 does not describe a feeling about generosity. It describes wealth actually moving — and Abu Bakr's giving was a great amount of his money, spent on strangers in chains.

**Who receives it.** Abu Qahāfah's advice was worldly common sense: invest in the strong. Abu Bakr kept freeing those who were, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, generally weak and helpless — people who had done him no past favour at all. The transaction stayed entirely between him and Allah.

**Why.** Ayah 20 leaves only one permitted answer, and Abu Bakr had already given it in his own words: not to expect any benefit in return, but to seek the pleasure of Allah. Ibn Kathir raises the horizon further still — the hope of seeing Him in the Gardens of Paradise.

And ayah 21 is the consolation for everyone who does this and sees nothing come back. *He, surely, will be pleased.* Not necessarily now. But surely.
